items.prompt: How does a moss take in the water it needs?

options.label: Through roots reaching into the soil
options.feedback: A moss has no true roots — only fine rhizoids that anchor it, and they are not built to carry water upward.

options.label: Through its whole leafy surface
options.feedback: With no roots, no tubes, and no waxy coat, every leaf cell can take up moisture the instant it touches the plant.

options.label: Through a stem that stores it in a reservoir
options.feedback: No moss stem holds a private supply of water; there is no reservoir to store it in.

options.label: Through spores drifting in humid air
options.feedback: Spores are for spreading the plant, not for feeding it; they play no part in taking up water.

items.ok_line: No pipes needed when every cell can drink for itself.
items.ko_line: Look for what a moss lacks, not what it might have instead.
items.exp_text: A moss has no roots, no internal tubes, and no waterproof coating, so each leaf simply takes up moisture the instant it touches the plant — rain, dew, or even damp air — much as a paper towel does. Because nothing inside carries water from one part to another, every leaf must fend for itself, taking in what it needs and losing it again just as easily when the surface dries.

items.prompt: What makes a moss capsule open to release its spores at just the right moment?

options.label: A timer set by the plant's age
options.feedback: A moss capsule has no internal clock; its opening tracks the weather in the moment, not a fixed age.

options.label: Insects that chew the capsule open
options.feedback: No insect is required to open it — the capsule manages the job on its own, with no visitor needed.

options.label: Teeth around its rim that flex with humidity
options.feedback: Each tooth bends outward as it dries and curls shut again in damp air, opening the capsule only when spores can actually be carried off.

options.label: The stalk snapping once it dries out
options.feedback: The stalk holds the capsule aloft and does not break; the opening happens at the tip, not by the stalk failing.

items.ok_line: A door built out of teeth that bend with the air.
items.ko_line: The capsule reads the weather itself — nothing outside it is doing the work.
items.exp_title: Teeth that open only in dry weather
items.exp_text: Ringing the mouth of a ripe moss capsule is a row of teeth that bend outward as the air dries and curl back inward when it turns damp, since each tooth is built of cells that shrink unevenly as they lose water. Spores only slip out through the gaps when the teeth are open, which keeps them from being released into wet air where they would clump together and fall straight to the ground instead of drifting off.

items.prompt: Why can a shriveled, brown patch of moss turn green again minutes after rain falls on it?

options.label: It was never really dry, only dusty
options.feedback: A dry moss cushion is not merely dusty on the surface; its cells genuinely lose almost all their water.

options.label: New moss grows in over the old, dead patch
options.feedback: Nothing regrows that fast. The same plant that looked dead is the one turning green again.

options.label: Rain washes a layer of dirt off green tissue underneath
options.feedback: There is no hidden green layer under the dirt; the brown color is the moss's own cells shutting down, not a coating on top of them.

options.label: Its cells can dry out completely and still survive
options.feedback: Rather than protecting itself from drying, a moss cell lets itself dry out completely and simply restarts once water returns.

items.ok_line: A plant that can stop living and start again.
items.ko_line: The brown moss really was as dry and inactive as it looked.
items.exp_text: A moss cell has no built-in supply of water to protect it from drought, so instead it lets itself dry out completely, folding its inner membranes into a stable, dormant state rather than tearing apart as most cells would. The moment water touches the tissue again, those membranes unfold and the cell's machinery restarts, which is why a patch that looked dead can be photosynthesizing again before the puddle it sat in has dried.

items.prompt: What is a lichen actually made of?

options.label: A single organism related to moss
options.feedback: A lichen is not one organism and not a relative of moss; it is a partnership between two very different kinds of life.

options.label: A fungus growing on top of dead moss
options.feedback: A lichen is not simply a fungus using dead moss as a surface; the living partner inside it is not moss at all.

options.label: A type of coral that lives on land
options.feedback: Coral is an animal that builds a hard skeleton in the sea; a lichen shares neither trait.

options.label: A fungus and an alga living as one
options.feedback: The fungus builds the structure and holds water, while the alga or bacterium inside photosynthesizes and feeds them both.

items.ok_line: Neither could look like this alone.
items.ko_line: The lichen you're looking at is really two organisms sharing one body.
items.exp_text: A lichen forms when a fungus surrounds a population of algae or light-capturing bacteria and builds a shared body around them: the fungus supplies the structure, holds water, and shields the partner from strong light, while the alga or bacterium photosynthesizes and feeds them both. Neither one grown alone looks anything like the lichen, since the crusty or leafy shape only appears once the two are locked together.

items.prompt: How can a lichen growing on a bare rock help turn that rock into soil?

options.label: It secretes acids that slowly dissolve minerals in the rock
options.feedback: Those acids loosen mineral grains in the rock's surface, grains that eventually become the first thin layer of soil.

options.label: It flattens the rock's surface as it spreads
options.feedback: Spreading across a surface does not flatten it; the rock's shape is unaffected by the lichen's outline.

options.label: It drops seeds into cracks that widen as they grow
options.feedback: A lichen has no seeds. Whatever a lichen releases to reproduce is not a seed with roots that could pry a rock apart.

options.label: It absorbs the rock's minerals directly
options.feedback: Nothing about direct absorption would loosen the rock; the mineral would need to be broken down first.

items.ok_line: Rock into grit, one lichen at a time.
items.ko_line: The lichen isn't breaking the rock apart physically — it's changing it chemically.
items.exp_text: The fungal partner in a lichen releases weak acids onto the rock it clings to, and those acids slowly pull minerals out of the stone's surface, loosening grains that would otherwise stay locked together for far longer. Over time those loosened grains, mixed with the remains of the lichen itself once it dies, become the first thin layer of soil that later plants can take root in.

items.prompt: Why are lichens often the first living things to disappear when air pollution rises in a city?

options.label: They need shade and cities are too bright
options.feedback: Light levels in a city are not the problem; plenty of lichens thrive in full sun elsewhere.

options.label: They are eaten by pigeons that gather in cities
options.feedback: Lichens are not a food pigeons rely on, and their disappearance has nothing to do with being eaten.

options.label: They have no roots or waxy coating to filter what settles on them
options.feedback: With nothing to filter what touches it, a lichen absorbs pollutants right along with the water and minerals it actually needs.

options.label: They need soil, and cities pave it over
options.feedback: Many lichens grow directly on bark or bare rock and never touch soil at all, so paving is not what removes them.

items.ok_line: Whatever is in the air ends up in the lichen.
items.ko_line: A lichen has no barrier between itself and the air around it.
items.exp_text: A lichen takes in water and minerals across its entire surface, since it has no roots, no waxy skin, and no way to close itself off the way a leaf can, and whatever is dissolved in the rain or drifting in the air is absorbed right along with what the lichen actually needs. Pollutants build up inside its tissue instead of being kept out, which is why a lichen growing near heavy traffic can stop growing well before the trees around it show any sign of harm.

items.prompt: Why does a mat of moss stay damp long after the rain around it has dried up?

options.label: It has deep roots pulling up groundwater
options.feedback: Moss has no roots that reach groundwater; whatever is retained is held near the surface, not pumped up from below.

options.label: Its densely packed cushion holds water between the individual plants
options.feedback: The narrow gaps between thousands of tightly packed shoots draw water in and hold it there by capillary action.

options.label: It is coated in a layer of natural wax
options.feedback: A waxy coating would stop water from getting in at all; moss instead relies on being freely open to water.

options.label: It photosynthesizes water out of the air
options.feedback: Photosynthesis uses water as a raw material — it does not produce water out of the air.

items.ok_line: Thousands of tiny plants holding one shared puddle.
items.ko_line: It isn't pulling water from below — it's trapping water among itself.
items.exp_title: Held between the stems, not inside them
items.exp_text: A moss cushion is made of thousands of tiny shoots packed tightly side by side, and the narrow gaps between them draw water in and hold it there by capillary action, the same pull that lets a thin tube suck liquid upward against gravity. Because that trapped water sits between the plants rather than evaporating freely from an open surface, the whole cushion stays moist long after a bare patch of ground nearby has dried.

items.prompt: How does Sphagnum moss manage to hold many times its own weight in water?

options.label: Its leaves are wrapped in a thin, sealed membrane
options.feedback: A sealed membrane would keep water out rather than drawing it in and holding it.

options.label: It grows in standing water and never actually dries
options.feedback: Sphagnum can and does dry out at its surface; its water-holding trick works even away from standing water.

options.label: Most of its cells are dead, hollow, and built to soak up water
options.feedback: Those dead, hollow cells fill with water through small holes in their walls and hold a reservoir far larger than the plant's living tissue.

options.label: It secretes a gel that coats the surrounding ground
options.feedback: The moss does not coat the ground around it; the water is held inside the plant's own structure.

items.ok_line: A sponge the plant builds and then empties out.
items.ko_line: Look inside the leaf itself for where the water is actually kept.
items.exp_title: A plant that is mostly empty cells
items.exp_text: Most of the cells in a Sphagnum leaf die on purpose as the leaf matures, leaving behind an empty, porous shell with small holes in its wall, and those dead cells sit beside the few living ones that keep the plant growing. Water floods into the dead cells through the holes and stays trapped there, which lets a single plant hold a reservoir far larger than its own living tissue and keep the ground beneath it waterlogged even in a dry spell.

items.prompt: Why does a moss need a film of rainwater on its surface in order to reproduce?

options.label: The sperm must swim through the water to reach the egg
options.feedback: Moss sperm can only travel to a waiting egg by swimming through a continuous film of water connecting the two plants.

options.label: The spores dissolve in dry air without water
options.feedback: Spores are built to survive dry air; that stage of the moss's life is not the one needing the water.

options.label: Water carries pollen from one plant to another
options.feedback: Moss has no pollen or flowers; that is a mechanism belonging to seed plants, not moss.

options.label: The water washes away rival mosses nearby
options.feedback: Rainwater does not clear away competitors; nothing about reproduction depends on other mosses being removed.

items.ok_line: No rain, no journey, no offspring.
items.ko_line: The water isn't needed for spreading spores — it's needed earlier than that.
items.exp_title: A journey that only water allows
items.exp_text: A moss makes swimming sperm rather than pollen, and those sperm can only travel from where they are released to a waiting egg on a neighboring plant by swimming through a continuous film of water, exactly as their distant algal ancestors did. Without rain or dew to connect the two plants, the sperm have nowhere to swim and no egg is ever fertilized, which is why thick moss cushions crowd close together instead of spreading out.

items.prompt: Why do some lichens lie completely flat against a rock while others stand up in branching tufts?

options.label: The flat ones are younger and still growing into the tufted shape
options.feedback: A flat lichen does not turn into a branching one as it ages; each keeps the same growth form throughout its life.

options.label: Different lichens attach to their surface in different ways
options.feedback: A crust-like lichen fuses flat against the rock while a branching one anchors at only a few points and grows upward into open air.

options.label: Wind wears the branching ones down over time until they lie flat
options.feedback: Wind does not reshape one form into another; both forms exist side by side regardless of local wind.

options.label: Flat lichens are dead and tufted ones are alive
options.feedback: A flat, crust-like lichen is just as alive as a branching one; flatness is not a sign of death.

items.ok_line: One glued flat, one standing free.
items.ko_line: The shape is built in from the start, not something that changes over a lichen's life.
items.exp_title: Built to hug, or built to reach
items.exp_text: A crust-like lichen grows fused directly to the rock across its entire underside, giving it no room to lift away, while a branching lichen anchors at only a few points and grows its body upward and outward into the open air. The flat form survives fierce scouring wind and baking sun exactly where it sits, and the branching form instead reaches past the still air at the rock's surface to catch more light and moisture.
